reason: The narrative presents the opposite dynamic. King Ahab and the priests of Baal (the leaders) are clearly depicted as being in the wrong—Elijah explicitly tells Ahab that he and his house have abandoned God's commandments and followed Baal (אַתָּה וּבֵית אָבִיךָ בַּעֲזָבְכֶם אֶת־ מִצְוֺת יְהוָה). The regular people, while initially wavering and indecisive (פֹּסְחִים עַל־ שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים—'limping between two opinions'), ultimately demonstrate they are right by correctly recognizing God after the divine fire consumes the sacrifice, declaring יְהוָה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים (The Lord, He is God) and obeying Elijah's command. The text shows the people's eventual alignment with truth, not their wrongness.
